b: the stair down with lamps lit, two landings in four hundred steps, the carvings on the wall going from mason's work to something cut in a hurry by hands that were not dwarves, and on the second landing a stair-shrine with nine niches in it
c: Stop at the shrine and read it.
Take twenty minutes on the first landing; they need it.

b: four hundred steps in the dark with a hand on the wall, the carvings changing under the palm from tool-work to gouges, and at the ninetieth step something coming up past the company on the outside of the stair, unhurried, breathing on a count
c: Press flat to the wall and let it pass.
Strike a light; blind is worse than seen.
Count the steps aloud to keep the company together.
Take hold of it as it goes by.

b: the stair roped and Kettle a flight ahead working on tugs: one for clear, two for wait, three for come. She gives one, one, one, and then two, and then the rope goes slack in your hands with no signal at all
c: Go down fast on the last signal she gave.
Overtake the slack and take the lead yourself.
Haul the rope in and see what is on the end of it.

b: the stair-shrine: nine niches cut at eye height, eight holding dwarf tokens black with age, the ninth empty and warm enough to feel from a foot away, and a groove worn in the shrine's lip by something set there and taken back many times
c: Leave the ninth niche empty and go down.
Set the ninth iron in the empty niche.
Take one of the eight tokens.

b: the ninth iron set in the warm niche, which accepts it the way a lock accepts a key, and the whole hill going quiet for the length of a breath before the count starts again somewhere below, slower, satisfied, and no longer interested in the company
c: Go down and see what you have bought.

b: a lamp struck on the stair and the thing on the outside of the flight caught in it for one second: a Warden's cloak, a Warden's boots, and above the collar nothing that a helmet would fit, going up past you without turning
c: Go down before it comes back for a second look.

b: the slack rope followed down two flights and Kettle found flat against the wall with her hand over her own mouth, alive, furious, and pointing at the stairfoot where a work-gang of Fenkin is carrying crates in file across the bottom of the stair
c: Wait for the file to pass and go down.

b: the foot of the great stair, a crossing of ways in warm moving air: a flooded gallery to the left with lamplight on the water, the pay-hall doors ahead standing ajar, a chapel light off to the right, the sound of a mill wheel turning somewhere below, a breach in the wall where the vault cuts into the old barrow, a cutting-shop with a cold forge, and at the far end of everything a door
c: Go and find the wheel that is turning.
Look into the breach in the wall.
Straight down the hall to the door at the end.
Hail the garrison; somebody down here must be Warden.

b: the flooded gallery, chest-deep and warm as bathwater, lamplight further down it and a flat-bottomed ferry poling toward you with three Fenkin aboard and a crate lashed amidships that is not making crate noises
c: Swim the gallery past them in the dark water.
Take the ledge above the waterline.
Ambush the ferry from both sides.
Go under and hole the ferry from below.

b: sixty yards of warm black water with kit held over the head, the ferry's pole going by an arm's length away, and something long turning over in the depth beneath the company with the unhurried indifference of the very well fed
c: Get out at the far steps and keep going.
Take a breath and see what is under you.

b: the ledge above the waterline, eleven inches wide, cut for maintenance and not for men in mail, with the ferry passing below close enough to hear the crate being spoken to in a language of numbers
c: Work along it to the far end.
Drop on the ferry as it passes underneath.
Take the shortcut where the ledge is broken.

b: eleven seconds of violence in waist-deep water and three Fenkin dead over the gunwale, and then the crate: eighteen inches of dwarf oak with air holes bored in a ring of nine, and inside it something that has stopped making noise in order to listen to you
c: Leave it sealed and take the ferry down the gallery.
Free what is in it, whatever it is.
Take the gang's lamps and pass as the work-file.

b: the crate opened: a Warden of the second relief patrol, alive, wrists bound in the Compact's knot, blindfolded and counting under his breath in a rhythm the company has heard three times today and never wanted to hear from a human throat
c: Cut him loose, take him with you, and go.
Ask him what he is counting toward.

b: the crate's lid levered off and the bound Warden inside cut free and carried, dead weight and counting, while Nyre holds his head and tells him the number is wrong, over and over, which is the only argument anyone has
c: Carry him and go on to the door.

b: three Fenkin lamps held at Fenkin height and the company poling a ferry down a flooded dwarf gallery in the middle of a work-file that does not look up, learning by watching what the crates are for, where they go, and how often
c: Tie up at the door steps and get off the water.

b: the deep pay-hall, ankle-deep and echoing: a rack on the far wall holding eight key-irons in eight sockets, a ninth socket empty, the pay-bell on its stand, and the paymaster himself face down across his own table with both sleeves empty from the elbow
c: Take the eight irons off the rack.
Read the tally cut into the wall behind the rack.
Ring the pay-bell and see who still answers it.

b: the paymaster turned over: no hands, no violence anywhere else, and inside his coat a confession written in a hand that had to hold the pen in its teeth, saying that the ninth hand must be a hand that signs, that he signed for nine years, and that he stopped
c: Take the confession and the irons.
Take the confession and go straight to the door.
Look for what happened to his hands.

b: the rack up close: eight key-irons, each cut with a tally, each seated in a socket that is warm, and the ninth socket empty and worn bright, and the whole rack humming very faintly the way a bowstring hums before it is loosed
c: Take one iron and leave the seven seated.
Leave them all exactly where they are.
Take all eight; the Marshal can have the lot.

b: one iron lifted out and the rack's hum going up a tone, seven irons taking the strain of the eighth's absence, and Ilsabet saying, quietly and with great precision, that the company now has eleven minutes of the hill's patience and not a second more

the tally cut into the wall behind the rack, kept in nines, going back nine hundred years in nine hands and then further in a hand that is not dwarf work at all, and the last group having eight strokes cut and a ninth begun
c: Stop reading and go to the door.
Read it to the end; there is a name at the bottom.

b: the chapel of the Compact: nine benches, a wall of tally, and at a clerk's writing desk a courteous grey man in a good coat who stands as the company comes in, greets them as the Ninth Sword by name and by number, and offers the captain the only chair
c: Hear the offer he means to make.
Ask what the Compact actually pays, and to whom.
Put him down where he stands.
Back out and go and find the wheel instead.
Put a lamp against his tally-wall and burn it.

b: Coren Vale explains the arithmetic like a factor explaining interest: the thing behind the door is not killable and not wakeable while the count holds, eight irons hold the lid, the ninth hand keeps the count and delivers what is owed, and the frontier has been paying that instalment for nine hundred years
c: Let him make his offer, then.
Leave him talking and go to the door.

b: the offer, made plainly and without threat: Vale is ninety-one years old and tired, the ninth hand's place is vacant on his death, and he will give the company the iron, the ledger, the garrison's back pay and nine years of the frontier's peace for one of the five, named by the captain, today
c: Refuse, and go for the door.
Counter: the company will settle this another way.
Accept, and name one of them.

b: the counter-offer put to him: the company will close the door properly, all nine irons seated and no hand at all keeping any count, and Vale's face doing something complicated because in ninety-one years nobody has proposed it, and he is not certain it cannot be done
c: Go to the door with his blessing, such as it is.

b: Vale does not defend himself, and does not need to: the chapel does it for him, nine benches worth of dust standing up in the shapes of the people who sat on them, and Dellach's first swing going through a grey man's coat and hitting the desk behind it
c: Finish him before the benches close.
Break off and run for the door.
Take him hostage and walk him to the door.

b: Coren Vale killed at his own desk in the time it takes to say a number, and the count stopping: not slowing, stopping, everywhere in the hill at once, and in the silence afterwards the sound of eight irons taking a load they were never asked to take alone
c: Run for the door now, while the silence lasts.
Take his tally-book and his ring off the desk.
Wait and see what the count does without a keeper.

b: Vale's tally-book and the ninth hand's ring taken off a dead man's desk, the book eleven hundred pages of instalments in nine hands, the last of them his, and the ring warm and sized, unmistakably, for whoever picks it up
c: Take both and go to the door.

b: the wheel-house under the pay-hall: a dwarf pump the size of a barn, its wheel turning in a race of black water, three of its nine paddles hacked away and a Fenkin crew working on the fourth with axes and no hurry at all
c: Kill the crew and mend the paddles.
Jam the wheel and flood the deep yourselves.
Cross the wheel-race to the door gallery.
Ride the wheel down and see what it drains into.

b: a short brutal fight in a loud room and then an hour of carpentry, Dellach and Odd holding a paddle while Ilsabet lashes it, the water in the race dropping a hand's width, the deep staying dry a while longer for whatever that is worth
c: Leave it running and go to the door.
Stay and keep it running; somebody has to.

b: the wheel jammed with a poleaxe haft and the race backing up in minutes, water going the wrong way through nine hundred years of dwarf engineering and down into the lower hall where the crates are stacked and the work-file is still working
c: Do it and run for the door on the high side.
Do it now, while half the company is still below.

b: the wheel-race crossed on the axle housing with the wheel turning a foot from the back of your head, nine paddles coming round, the gap between them exactly as wide as a man who does not hesitate
c: Cross one at a time on the count of the paddles.
Cross together and quickly; the crew has seen you.

b: the breach in the vault wall, and behind it the barrow the dwarves cut into and thought they had merely cut into: a king's chamber with nine attendants seated round a king who is not there, their plaques still legible, their hands all pointing the same way
c: Close the breach with rubble and be done with it.
Go through the barrow to the door gallery.
Take the ring off the empty king's chair.

b: nine plaques read in order, and they are not names but offices: the one who counts, the one who carries, the one who signs, and so on to the ninth, which is the one who is owed, and all nine hands pointing at the chamber's inner door
c: Go to the door with that in your head.
Follow where all nine hands are pointing.

b: two hours of rubble and mortar dust and Dellach's shoulder against a slab, the breach closed as well as five people can close it, and the certain knowledge in everyone that this is housekeeping and not a solution

through the barrow's inner chamber toward the door gallery, past nine empty attendant chairs and one that is occupied by something that has been sitting patiently since before the dwarves cut the first gallery, and that does not turn its head as you pass
c: Walk past it without looking and keep walking.
Look at it properly, once, so you know.

b: the cutting-shop where the irons were made: a cold forge, a tally-die bolted to an anvil, racks of blanks gone to rust, the cutting-orders still pinned to the bench, and a dwarf smith folded up under the bellows with his tools laid out in order beside him
c: Cut a blank into a ninth iron on the die.
Take the tally-die off the anvil.
Read the cutting-orders on the bench.
Light the forge; you need the heat and the light.

b: three hours of cold work with a die that wants a striker and a smith, Ilsabet reading the tally-order aloud stroke by stroke while Dellach swings, and at the end of it a ninth key-iron that is nine parts right and one part yours
c: Take it and go to the door.
Cut a second one while the die is set.

b: the tally-die unbolted and wrapped, forty pounds of dwarf steel that decides what a key-iron says, which Ilsabet points out is either the most valuable thing in the hill or the most dangerous, and is certainly both
c: Carry it and go to the door.

b: the cutting-orders read off the bench: nine irons commissioned by the legion at the founding, eight to be cut with the holding tally, the ninth to be cut with a name left blank, to be filled in by the hand that would keep the count, and a note that the blank must never be cut twice
c: Take the orders and go to the door.

b: the Ninefold Door at the end of everything: dwarf iron in a frame of older stone, nine sockets in a ring, eight of them filled and warm, the ninth empty and worn bright, the metal of the door itself moving very slightly outward and back on a nine-count that the company has been hearing all day without naming, and behind it, patient, enormous, something that is not asleep and is not awake
c: Set the ninth iron in its socket and lock the door.
Draw the eight irons and unmake the Compact.
Take the ninth iron out of the hill entirely.
Open the door a hand's width and look.
Withdraw. This is a Warden matter and a Ledger crime.
Knock, the way you knocked at the gate.
Walk out of the hill and never speak of it again.

b: twenty minutes on the first landing with boots off, which the keeper's board warned against in chalk, and the stair's own traffic arriving on schedule to find a company sitting in the middle of a right of way that has been in continuous use for nine hundred years

a token lifted out of the second niche, and the seven remaining tokens all turning a quarter turn in their sockets at once, and the stair below the company filling with the sound of somebody coming up two flights at a time to correct an error

the steps counted aloud in the dark to keep five people together, which works until the count reaches nine and a second voice takes over the counting from somewhere below, and the company keeps descending because the numbers keep coming and they are correct

a hand put out to take hold of what is passing on the stair, and the discovery that it is willing to be held, and that it has been waiting a long time for somebody to initiate the transaction rather than merely submit to it

the rope hauled in hand over hand and coming up cut clean at forty feet, no scout, no signal, and the company climbing back up four hundred steps to a hillside in daylight to write a letter to a fen family about somebody who went down first because she always went down first

e: capture|negative|Somebody Down Here Must Be Warden
b: a hail sent down a dwarf hall in the Warden's form, and the answer coming back correctly from six directions at once in six voices the company heard reading a duty roster upstairs, and the lamps in the flooded gallery all turning together toward the stair

the ferry holed from underneath and going down in eight feet of warm water with its crate, and the crate opening as it sinks, and whatever the Compact had packed in it deciding, reasonably, that the nearest hands in the water will do

one breath taken and one look down into warm black water with a lamp held under the surface, and the thing that has been turning over below the company all this time turning over once more, unhurriedly, to look back up

the broken span of the ledge taken as a shortcut on the reasonable assumption that dwarf stone fails slowly, which it does, except where nine hundred years of warm water have been working at the mortar from underneath

the bound Warden asked what he is counting toward, and answering, in detail, in a voice that becomes several voices, and the lamps down the gallery stopping their work to listen to the answer with the company still standing in the water

the pay-bell rung once in a deep hall, which is what a pay-bell is for, and the garrison answering it: eleven of them from the barracks wall, the paymaster's clerks from the flooded gallery, and all of them forming up in the old order to be paid

a search for a dead paymaster's hands, which are found, still working, set in the wall's tally-groove where they have been cutting the same nine strokes over and over for eleven years, and which stop when they are noticed

eight key-irons pulled out of eight warm sockets in under a minute by a company that came here for salvage, and the Ninefold Door doing exactly what nine hundred years of dwarf engineering was arranged to prevent it from doing

the wall-tally read to the bottom of the last group, where the ninth stroke has been begun and not finished, and where a name is cut beside it in fresh work: not the paymaster's, not Vale's, but the name of whoever is reading

a lamp broken against nine hundred years of accounts and the chapel going up in a light that shows what is sitting on all nine benches, and Vale standing in the middle of it entirely unharmed, apologising, and explaining that the tally is not kept on the wall

a name spoken aloud in a warm chapel, and Vale writing it in his book without hurry, and the company walking out of the hill four strong and rich with the frontier safe for nine years, which is a real thing that was really bought, and which none of the four can look at

the captain's own name written in the ninth hand's book, the company sent up the stair with the ledger, the iron, and the back pay, and a new keeper sitting down at a clerk's desk to learn a count that has been running for nine hundred years and will not be finishing soon

Coren Vale walked to the Ninefold Door at knifepoint as surety, entirely cooperative, faintly amused, and explaining on the way that a hostage is only worth what the other party is unwilling to lose, and that the thing behind the door has never been unwilling to lose anything

a stand made in a chapel against nine benches of standing dust, which is a fight the company wins for ninety seconds and loses for the reason Vale did not bother to mention, that everyone who has ever sat in that room is still on the roll

the silence after Vale's death waited out to see what a count does without a keeper, and the answer arriving from the direction of the door: it looks for the nearest hand that has held an iron today, and it is not particular about consent

a ride down the wheel-race on a paddle to see where the water goes, which is a shaft, and then a sump, and then a chamber that the dwarves pumped out for nine hundred years for a reason they wrote down in three places

the company staying at the pump because the deep must be kept dry, working shifts on dwarf machinery, and the door business left for the Wardens, who will come in spring, and who will find a wheel in good order and nobody at it

the wheel jammed on the captain's word with Kettle and Odd still on the low side of the race, and nine hundred years of held water going where it has always wanted to go, faster than anybody can climb
the wheel-race crossed together and quickly with a Fenkin crew shouting behind, which puts two people in the gap at once, and the gap between paddles is exactly one person wide and always has been

a ring taken off the arm of a chair that has no king in it, and the nine attendants round the chamber turning their heads together to see who has accepted the office, and the plaque under the ninth chair being, it turns out, a job description

one long look at the occupied chair, taken deliberately so that at least one person in the company would know what was in the room, and the thing in the chair returning the courtesy in full and at length

a dwarf forge lit for the first time in nine hundred years because the company wanted heat and light, and the flue of it running, as dwarf flues do, straight up into the pay-hall and straight down into the door gallery, announcing the work to everything that has ever worked here

a second ninth iron cut on a die whose own orders say the blank must never be cut twice, and the hill's arithmetic acquiring, in the space of one stroke, a tenth hand that it has no socket for and no intention of tolerating

three knocks on the Ninefold Door, which worked so well at the gate, and the door answering them: three from the other side, in the same rhythm, at a scale that moves dust off the ceiling and opinion out of everyone present

four hundred steps back up, the gap in the gate, the moor, and Gallowmere by the second evening, with a report that says the vault is unsafe and nothing else, and five people who will spend the rest of their lives not talking about the same afternoon

the door gallery, the last hundred yards: nine niches with nine lamps lit and trimmed, the air moving in and out along the floor on a nine-count, and at the halfway point a pair of Warden's boots set neatly against the wall with the tags still in them
c: Walk it, lamps up, and do not stop.
Put out your own lamps and walk it in the dark.
Take the tags out of the boots; somebody's family gets a name.

b: two Warden tags lifted out of a pair of boots that were set down neatly by their owner in a place where nothing is neat by accident, and the nine lamps of the gallery going out in order from the far end, and the boots being, on reflection, a place setting
